In addition to these eastlake and stick style buildings (usually two-or three-story structures), Olinder also has several bungelow style and other residences dating from the 1920's, 1930's, and early 1940's. The development of the lots on the street grid likely occurred during this latter period, and with the exception that the landscape has since grown up, the neighborhood probably looks today like it did then.
Mention should also be made of a handsome white clapboard church, located at the corner of San Antonio and 20th Street, of 100-plus years in age. Isolated by Coyote Creek, the railroad, and heavily-trafficked streets, Olinder has largely eluded the modern intrusions to which the Campus area has been subject. The lack of through-traffic has allowed a sense of serenity to prevail. Like the wooden church, which has yet to be listed as an historical resource, Olinder is a charming and undiscovered district of San Jose's residential downtown.
I. SOCIO/ECONOMIC CHARACTER
The San Jose General Plan 1975, published in early 1976 contains a thorough description of the over-all social and economic character of the city and its residents. Relevant portions of that text are quoted below:
"The rapid economic development of the San Jose area has attracted primarily a young, working age population. As of the 1970 census, the median age was 24.4, mostly composed of families with children. In 1970, the average household size was 3.35 persons per household, which was among the highest of any major city in the United States.
San Jose residents tend to be affluent and highly mobile within the metropolitan area. The $10, 854 median family income in 1970 was among the nation's highest for large cities. San Joseans tend to be homeowners rather than renters.
Approximately 28% of San Jose's total population is classified as "minority", the highest percentage is of Spanish heritage. This Spanish-speaking population (22% of total) is mostly concentrated in the Central and Alum Rock Planning Areas, which have 53% of the total Spanish speaking population. Although in total number, (1305 total population) 65% of the Alviso population is Spanish-speaking.
The rising affluence of San Jose and the County is not uniformly distributed... Trend analysis suggests that the County's population is becoming more segregate residentially by income and ethnic group, while the affluent areas are experiencing greater per capita economic growth than the less affluent areas. San Jose is a socially and economically heterogenous community. In general, areas closer to the central core thend to have more social and economic problems. Willow Glen and Central Planning Areas have most of the housing built before 1950 and lower income rental units. Central is even less affluent, with the oldest housing in San Jose, a large number of single person households and rental units, and a higher rate of social problems. The planning area to the east such as Alum Rock, Berryessa and Evergreen approach the County norm in income and life-style in the area near the foothills. The portions closer to the central part of San Jose, however, have high minority composition and are generally less affluent.
